articles.summary: President Donald Trump's approval rating remained near its lowest-ever level ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, with a growing number of voters
articles.body: President Donald Trump's approval rating remained near its lowest-ever level ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, with a growing number of voters viewing their ballots as a chance to register opposition to the Republican leader, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found.The poll, completed on Monday, showed Democrats leading Republicans by eight percentage points on the generic congressional ballot, 46% to 38%, even as the gap narrowed from 11 points a week earlier.The findings point to mounting political challenges for Republicans, fuelled in part by soaring fuel prices following Trump's war on Iran in February. With all 435 seats in the House of Representatives at stake, Democrats are seen as having a stronger chance of reclaiming control of the chamber, while their path in the Senate remains tougher.Trump's approval rating at 32%Trump, though not on the ballot, remains a central figure in the election. Only 32% of respondents approved of his performance, unchanged from the previous week and just above his record low of 31% recorded two weeks ago.Among independent voters, 50% said their vote was intended to oppose Trump, while just 13% said it was a vote in his favour. Another 33% said the president was not a factor in their decision.Cost of living emerges as key election issueThe rising cost of living also emerged as a major electoral concern, with 78% saying it would be very important or the most important factor in deciding their vote. On the issue, Democrats led Republicans 43% to 32%.Democrats also appeared more motivated to vote, with 49% of their supporters describing themselves as very enthusiastic about voting, compared with 33% of Republican voters.The Reuters/Ipsos poll surveyed 1,765 US adults online and had a margin of error of two percentage points.Trump wrapped up his midterm campaign push on Monday with a rally at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC.He has no public appearances planned for Election Day, with his schedule showing a series of private meetings, including one with John Joseph Arrigo, the US ambassador to Portugal, the Associated Press reported. His schedule also includes a closed-door “signing time”, during which he typically signs executive orders, proclamations and bills passed by Congress.Trump is also scheduled to host an election night reception in the White House East Room, which is listed as closed to media coverage. articles.body: VISAKHAPATNAM: A fire that broke out at Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited's (HPCL) Visakhapatnam refinery in Malkapuram on Monday night was brought under control, with no casualties or injuries reported.The fire was confined to a pitch intermediate storage tank in the refinery's sulfur unit, and all units at the facility are operating safely, HPCL said.In a post on X, the company said the fire was reported around 10pm on November 2, following which its Fire and Safety Team immediately activated firefighting and emergency response measures."The fire was localised to the pitch tank area and was brought under control within a short time. articles.title: UK weather: largely dry start to November follows wet but sunny October
articles.summary: Provisional Met Office figures just released show the UK had a warmer, wetter and sunnier October than average but quieter weather has now arrived.
articles.body:
High pressure has seized control of the UK weather meaning largely dry, settled but chilly autumn conditions will continue this week.

Days will bring a mix of patchy cloud, sunny spells and a few showers, with frost and fog expected to form at night - especially in northern and western areas.

Temperatures will generally be around or a little below the seasonal norm and it will feel particularly chilly in southern England and south Wales where there will be a brisk easterly breeze.

The relatively quiet start to November follows a decidedly mixed October which - according to Met Office data just released was wetter, warmer and sunnier than average.

Provisional Met Office statistics show that the UK received 13% more rain overall than in a typical October.

All four nations had above average rainfall but the trend was particularly clear in northern Scotland, which came in 31% above the long-term average.

The wettest weather came during the final third of the month, especially as Storm Austen and Storm Boelo swept through.

The UK's joint-sixth wettest day on record was provisionally 24 October.

The Environment Agency said England had experienced its wettest week in two years but warned it was not enough to ease the ongoing drought.

Sustained above-average rainfall will be needed throughout the winter to counteract the effects of the hottest summer on record .

Rainfall was not the only element of October's weather story.

Sunshine amounts were above average for the UK as a whole - in fact it was the fifth-sunniest October since records began in 1910.

It was also a warm month with overall mean temperatures 0.9C above average.

The warmth was particularly notable in Shetland, which had its joint-sixth warmest October on record.

It marked the UK's ninth consecutive month of above-average temperatures.

The jet stream , which propelled Storms Austen and Boelo towards our shores, has now shifted north.

This has allowed high pressure to build, fending off major rain-bearing weather systems and keeping things predominantly dry through the first few days of November.

However, with high pressure centred across the north of the UK, a brisk easterly breeze will affect southern and eastern areas on Tuesday.

Gusts of 30-40mph are possible around some coasts and also for the Channel Islands.

The breeze will deliver a scattering of showers - most frequent in East Anglia and south-east England.

Many northern and western areas will stay dry though with early fog lifting to leave patchy cloud and sunny spells.

Temperatures will reach 11 to 13C but it will feel chillier than that in areas exposed to the wind.

Tuesday night will be rather cold with temperatures generally falling to between 3 and 7C, but possibly dipping below freezing in some rural parts of Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England - giving a touch of frost.

This is also where fog is most likely with some dense patches possible, whereas further south it is likely to be too breezy for mist or fog to form.

The same pattern will continue until the end of the week with overnight frost and fog most widespread in northern areas of the UK, and daytime sunny spells interspersed with showers.

Temperatures in many areas will drop by a degree or two.

It is likely that a relatively weak area of low pressure will drift northwards from France over the weekend increasing the chance that patchy rain will move across the UK.

This could be followed by another drier interlude early next week, but beyond that most computer models suggest that high pressure will decline, allowing Atlantic weather systems to return

This would mean wetter and windier weather but there is a lot of uncertainty - with no definite sign of any storms on the horizon.

articles.title: A Michigan nonprofit founder stole $1.4 million meant for vulnerable preschool children; the organisation eventually shut down and 35 employees lost their jobs
articles.summary: A Michigan nonprofit organisation that was set up to support vulnerable preschool children shut down after its founder diverted $1.4 million in taxpayer
articles.body: A Michigan nonprofit organisation that was set up to support vulnerable preschool children shut down after its founder diverted $1.4 million in taxpayer and donor funds for personal use. The fraud affected Early Learning Neighborhood Collaborative (ELNC), which provided essential services to children and families in some of the poorest communities in West Michigan. Its closure in 2023 left 35 employees without jobs and deprived several preschools of financial support. The founder, Nkechy Ezeh, was sentenced to more than 5 years in federal prison in May 2026.Michigan nonprofit founder stole $1.4 million meant for preschool childrenAccording to the US Department of Justice, Ezeh, 61, founded Early Learning Neighborhood Collaborative(ELNC) and served as its chief executive. The organisation received funding from government programmes and private donors to improve early childhood education in underserved communities.Its funding came from the federal Department of Health and Human Services' Early Head Start programme, the US Department of Education and 3 major charitable organisations in Michigan. The money was intended to support children who needed additional assistance during their early years.The nonprofit provided meals, transportation, financial assistance, advocacy and other services to children attending preschools in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. These resources were particularly important for families who could not easily afford additional childcare and educational support.However, prosecutors found that Ezeh had diverted approximately $1.4 million from the organisation for purposes unrelated to its work. The money included taxpayer funding and donations that were supposed to benefit young children and their families. The Department of Justice announced her sentence on May 13, 2026.How was the money allegedly spentThe investigation revealed that the money was used to support Ezeh's personal lifestyle rather than the organisation's educational programmes. According to the US Department of Justice, her spending included luxury holidays, family expenses and payments to relatives who were listed as employees despite doing little or no work.A report by CBS News Detroit detailed how Ezeh used money from the nonprofit to travel to Hawaii, Europe and Africa. She also used some of the funds to pay for a family member's wedding.One of the methods used in the scheme involved what investigators described as a ghost payroll. Ezeh placed family members on ELNC's payroll, allowing them to receive payments even though they performed little or no legitimate work for the organisation.According to prosecutors, these payments amounted to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The arrangement meant that money intended to provide practical support to preschool children was instead being channelled to people connected to the founder.The fraud also involved transfers to Nigeria. Prosecutors said Ezeh used intermediaries, commonly known as money mules, to send hundreds of thousands of dollars in stolen funds to her family members in the country.The impact on children and employeesThe consequences extended well beyond the organisation's finances. ELNC eventually closed its operations in 2023, leaving 35 employees without jobs. According to the Department of Justice, the workers were laid off without notice as the organisation shut down.The closure also affected preschools that had depended on the nonprofit for financial assistance and other resources. Several centres lost funding, while children and families who relied on its services were left without the support they had previously received.The Department of Justice highlighted the circumstances of the children affected by the closure. Most of those served by ELNC were children of colour under the age of 5. Around 72% lived below the federal poverty line, with many coming from some of the poorest neighbourhoods in Kent County, Kalamazoo and Battle Creek.These families were among those who stood to benefit most from the organisation's services. US Attorney Timothy VerHey said the money taken from the organisation could have supported hundreds of children across West Michigan.Ezeh's professional background and the investigationBefore the fraud case, Ezeh had a recognised position in Michigan's education and nonprofit sectors. She received the West Michigan Woman of the Year award in 2018 and was appointed twice to the executive committee of Michigan's Early Childhood Investment Corporation.She was also a tenured professor of education and had established ELNC to improve early childhood support in underserved communities.According to the International Centre for Investigative Reporting(ICIR), Ezeh eventually admitted that she had conspired to steal approximately $1.4 million from ELNC and its donors between 2017 and 2023. She entered a guilty plea to wire fraud and tax evasion charges as part of an agreement with prosecutors.Ezeh's former bookkeeper, Sharon Killebrew, was also prosecuted for her involvement in the scheme. The Department of Justice said Killebrew was sentenced to 54 months in federal prison in November 2025 for her role as a co-conspirator.The court orders prison time and financial repaymentOn May 13, 2026, Chief US District Judge Hala Y. Jarbou sentenced Ezeh to 70 months in federal prison for the fraud scheme. She also received a concurrent 60-month sentence for evading income taxes, meaning the two prison terms will be served at the same time.The court ordered her to pay $1.4 million in restitution to the victims of the fraud, along with an additional $390,174 to the Internal Revenue Service. She was taken into custody immediately to begin serving her sentence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: PUNE: A 29-year-old woman, daughter-in-law of a prominent businessman in Pune, was found hanging from a ceiling fan in a flat in Mukund Nagar on Monday
articles.body: PUNE: A 29-year-old woman, daughter-in-law of a prominent businessman in Pune, was found hanging from a ceiling fan in a flat in Mukund Nagar on Monday morning, following an alleged dispute with her mother-in-law.Police arrested her husband and registered a case of harassment and abetment of suicide against four members of her in-laws' family after her relatives accused them of subjecting her to harassment over repeated demands for gold.According to news agency PTI, the deceased, Payal Zambre Patil, was an IT professional before she quit her job.She was married to Akshay Zambre Patil, and the couple has a three-year-old daughter.Senior inspector Yashwant Nikam of Swargate police station said Payal lived with her in-laws in Mukund Nagar, off Pune-Satara Road. On Monday morning, she allegedly sent messages to some people stating that her mother-in-law would be responsible if anything happened to her.Police said Payal had an argument with her mother-in-law on Sunday and left her matrimonial home. Her family and in-laws began searching for her on Monday morning. She was eventually found hanging from a ceiling fan in another flat in an apartment complex near their residence. The incident came to light around 11.30am."When police reached the apartment, she was found hanging from the ceiling. No suicide note was found," a Swargate police station official said, adding that statements of her maternal relatives were being recorded.Payal's brother, Rishikesh Pawar, alleged that her husband and in-laws appeared unconcerned when he reached their home on Monday morning. He claimed they began searching for her only after the family questioned them.According to Pawar, the in-laws returned within five minutes and informed them that Payal was in a nearby apartment. He alleged that the flat's door was locked from inside and he managed to enter through the rear balcony, where he found his sister hanging.He further claimed that Payal had repeatedly complained about harassment by her mother-in-law. Recalling Sunday's argument, Pawar said he had called Akshay and told him that the dispute was temporary and could be resolved.Payal's uncle alleged that she had been harassed over demands for gold since her marriage. He claimed her in-laws demanded 10 tolas of gold every Diwali."This year too, they demanded gold, but we told them that we were farmers and, given the drought-like situation, it was not possible for us to meet the demand. We had even promised to give the gold next year," he alleged.The complaint filed by Payal's family also accused her husband and in-laws of mentally harassing her during her pregnancy in 2022 by pressuring her to give birth to a boy. After she delivered a girl on March 30, 2023, her in-laws allegedly argued with her at the hospital and said they would not take responsibility for either her or the child, the complaint stated.Following her death, relatives from Payal's parental family allegedly vandalised her in-laws' residence, office and marriage hall, triggering tension in the area. Her father-in-law owns a marriage hall and an eatery on Pune-Satara Road, police said. Her parental family runs a business in the Khed-Shivapur area.Swargate police registered a case of harassment and abetment of suicide against four people, including Payal's husband and mother-in-law. Senior inspector Nikam said Akshay had been arrested and two police teams were formed to trace the remaining accused.While Payal's family has alleged that she was murdered and her death staged as suicide, police have registered a case of abetment of suicide. articles.title: A woman from Canada discovered she could whistle through her nose when she was just seven; decades later, LuLu Lotus set a world record with a nose whistle measuring 44.1 decibels
articles.summary: Over the internet, we have seen all kinds of records now. Among such witty talents, one such talent belongs to LuLu Lotus.
articles.body: Over the internet, we have seen all kinds of records now. Among such witty talents, one such talent belongs to LuLu Lotus. Her unusual talent earned her a place in the Guinness World Records for blowing a 44.1-decibel whistle using her nose. Guinness World Records terms it the loudest nose whistle in the world.LuLu first discovered her skill when she was just seven years old as a way to play pranks on her teachers and other students. LuLu said everyone used to scramble to pinpoint the source of the mysterious whistling sound, with one of the teachers even venturing into the hallway, convinced that it was coming from outside.What makes it even more interesting is that she can actually create melodious sounds using her nose. By using her throat muscles to control the flow of air, she allows sound to escape through her nose when her mouth is closed. Guinness World Records compares the sound to that of a bird call, which also has approximately a similar decibel level.Who'd have thought what started as a childhood prank would someday get her a record-breaking title?How a childhood prank became a Guinness World RecordThe turning point came in her life when she watched a documentary about DJ Steve Aoki, who held a Guinness World Record for being the most-travelled musician in one year. The documentary sparked her curiosity about whether her own unusual ability could earn her something, which led her to do some research, during which she found that Guinness actually has a category for the loudest nose whistle. She knew she wanted to attempt it.She began looking into the requirements and soon realised that measuring a nose whistle was not as easy as simply recording it on her phone. Guinness required specialised sound-measuring devices and a suitable soundproofed room for precision recording. After searching for help from various places, she approached Aercoustics Engineering Ltd. in Mississauga, whose team actually agreed to let her attempt the record free of charge.On June 3, 2022, LuLu officially secured the record with a whistle measuring 44.1 decibels, using a calibrated Brüel & Kjær 2250 sound level meter. During the attempt, she whistled the theme from The Godfather, one of her favourite tunes.For LuLu, the recognition was particularly meaningful, as she had grown up reading Guinness World Records and admiring people with unusual abilities, never imagining she'd herself make her name in the book someday.How does LuLu Lotus whistle through her nose?Since she shared her achievement, netizens have been curious about how she manages to do it, with many attempting to recreate the unusual whistle but failing to get the same results. While ordinary whistling requires air to pass through the mouth, LuLu has mastered a rather different technique by using her throat muscles to control the airflow and produce a sound through her nose.Unlike a conventional nose whistle, which may produce a simple high-pitched sound, LuLu can also control the pitch and rhythm to create recognisable tunes. During her Guinness World Records attempt, she demonstrated this by whistling the theme from The Godfather. What makes her ability particularly unusual is that she can produce these sounds without opening her mouth, turning something most people would struggle to do into a musical performance.Will LuLu Lotus attempt to break her own record? Following the achievement, LuLu has become an internet sensation herself, posting videos of herself attempting to whistle many songs and melodies, and the internet just cannot rest. In her conversation with Guinness World Records, she expressed an interest in breaking her own record someday. Interestingly, the unusual talent seems to run in the family, with her son picking up the skill. Her five-year-old son has also discovered how to whistle through his nose rather than his mouth. LuLu said it would be a dream come true if her son eventually broke her record.What began as a childhood trick to prank classmates and teachers has now become something she can share with her children, turning an unusual personal talent into a family heirloom.You use AI every day. articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
articles.summary: The ruling, which comes on the eve of the midterm elections, essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots in the state.
articles.body:
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.

The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.

Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.

The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.

The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.

"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.

Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.

California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.

What are the US midterms? A simple guide

The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.

About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.

In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".

On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.

California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.

They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible.

The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.

President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.

Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.

The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch".

With additional reporting by the BBC's David Willis

articles.title: US launches strikes on Iranian island ahead of election
articles.summary: US officials described the attacks on Qeshm Island as limited and defensive, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
articles.body:
The US has launched strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

Iranian state news agency IRNA reported several explosions on the island on Monday.

The US officials described the strikes as limited and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing upon a US aircraft.

The BBC has contacted US Central Command (Centcom), the part of the US military responsible for operations in the Middle East, for comment.

It comes ahead of the US midterm elections, which will determine whether the Republicans or Democrats control Congress.

Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Earlier on Monday, he told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.

"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."

He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe", a site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterm elections.

This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.

There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".

Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told IRNA earlier that "very intensive" talks to try and end the war are under way with the US via mediators.

He also said Tehran was prepared for both diplomatic and military scenarios "more than ever before" and that it was up to the US to choose between a "wise path" of negotiation or the "mistake of military aggression".

The Magic Foundation, founded by Julius Dein, the project aims to expand Olbolet Primary School from 130 to 375 students. The foundation says the school was the first in its area to combat female genital mutilation (FGM), but faces closure threats from the government over non-compliance with national education standards. Construction began in February 2026 and includes six new classrooms, electrification and sanitation facilities. articles.title: In 2021, businessman Steve Wilson and his wife bought a derelict Brisbane mansion for A$ 12.75 million; after spending about A$ 15 million, they restored its collapsed roof and grand rooms
articles.summary: In 2021, Steve and Jane Wilson purchased the derelict Lamb House in Brisbane for A$12.75 million and spent about A$15 million to restore its grandeur, turning a significant piece of history into their family home.
articles.body: For years, the red brick mansion on the Kangaroo Point cliffs was the sort of place Brisbane residents pointed to with a sigh. The roof had caved in, the walls were covered with graffiti and the landmark with sweeping river views was slowly falling apart. In 2021, one couple decided it would not end that way.How Lamb House fell into ruinLamb House, originally named “Home,” stands at 9 Leopard Street, Kangaroo Point, Brisbane. Designed by architect A.B. Wilson for John Lamb, the two-storey residence was built in 1902-03, according to Brisbane City Council’s heritage trail. Joy Lamb left the house in 2015 after parts of the roof collapsed and squatters later occupied the empty building and vandalised some of the original interior, RealCommercial reported. According to Real Estate Source, Brisbane City Council moved to sell the house to recover roughly A$300,000 in unpaid rates and went on the market in 2021.The couple who beat the developersSteve Wilson, businessman and chairman of Racing Queensland and his wife Jane purchased the 3,146-square-meter property in 2021 for A12.75 million, ABC News reported. It also stated that Steve and Jane outbid several competitors, including international offers and Brisbane developer Kevin Seymour. Heritage consultant Ben Gallet told ABC News that about $A15 million seemed a reasonable budget for a full renovation, while ABC Radio Brisbane reported that the land alone had been valued at more than A$6 million in 2019. But the final bill was far higher. When the Restoration Australia host Anthony Burke asked whether they had spent close to A$20 million, Wilson said it was not quite that much, Mediaweek reported.Construction started at what Wilson termed as the “save it” stage. The house was likened to a massive thunderstorm that could fall apart at any moment, its roof having collapsed. ABC Radio Brisbane also detailed the materials used in the renovation. Existing timber that could be salvaged was left in place, while other damaged parts were replaced with red cedar. Queensland hoop pine was used elsewhere in the house.Room and details rebuiltAccording to ABC News, the restored home has six bedrooms, a grand timber staircase, drawing rooms and morning rooms. AH Specialists also restored the rooms once used by maids and butlers. Vandals and thieves had stolen many of the historical elements, so craftsmen had to recreate the missing pieces.Stained glass specialists Gerry Cummins and Jill Stehn restored the laylight at the entrance over the impressive staircase. Little from the original laylight remained and the newly made one measures about two meters across and contains around one thousand pieces of glass, ABC News reported. Heritage plasterer Scott McMillan crafted the ceiling roses and molded cornices.A restorer’s second heritage projectThe Wilsons were already familiar with A.B. Wilson’s work. For roughly three decades, they had been working on Kinauld, an 1888 home designed by the same architect, ABC News reported. They also restored the house’s original name in place of the Lamb surname it carried for generations. Brisbane Open House has featured Lamb House in its private property tours, highlighting the residence’s architectural and historical significance. Brisbane Open House names Steve Wilson AM and Dr Jane Wilson AO as the owners who bought the property and oversaw its restoration. Network Rail said the work was an important part of a plan to support Sizewell C's transport strategy of 60% of all its materials being delivered by rail and sea.

articles.title: Suffolk murderer Steve Wright questioned about cold cases
articles.summary: Police say the 68-year-old is not currently a suspect in other cold cases.
articles.body:
Serial killer Steve Wright has been questioned about a series of cold cases but is "not currently a suspect" in any of them, the police have told the BBC.

The 68-year-old was jailed for life in 2008 for the murders of five women in Ipswich between October and December 2006.

In February, he was given a further life sentence after pleading guilty to the kidnap and killing of 17-year-old Victoria Hall , from Trimley St Mary, in September 1999.

Suffolk Police said his admissions prompted the force to consider whether Wright may have been involved in other unsolved disappearances or murders.

"Following his sentencing for the murder of Victoria Hall earlier this year, he has been interviewed in prison about other unsolved cases," a spokesperson said.

"In the cases where we have DNA we have sought to use it to eliminate him from inquiries."

Victoria had left the Bandbox nightclub in Felixstowe with her friend at about 01:00 BST in September 1999, and they went their separate ways at about 02:30.

After being reported missing the next day, her body was found five days later in a ditch 25 miles (40km) away in Creeting St Peter.

Wright was due to stand trial at the Old Bailey in London in February charged with murder and kidnap of Victoria, and of attempting to kidnap 22-year-old Emily Doherty.

However, he unexpectedly changed his plea to guilty, prompting gasps in the courtroom.

Prof David Wilson has suggested Wright may consider coming clean about potential links to other unsolved disappearances.

The prominent criminologist highlighted the cases of Kellie Pratt, 28, last seen in Norwich in 2000, and Amanda Duncan, 26, who went missing in Ipswich in 1993.

Police said they would not provide the details of the cases that officers quizzed Wright on when asked by the BBC.

"He is not currently a declared suspect on any unsolved case, but the potential for his involvement is always considered as we review cold cases," the police added.

The killer's admission to Victoria's murder came as a particular surprise given he has never admitted murdering any of the five women for which he was jailed nearly 20 years ago.

Wright was found guilty of murdering Tania Nicol, 19, Gemma Adams, 25, Anneli Alderton, 24, Paula Clennell, 24, Annette Nicholls, 29, on 21 February 2008.

He was sentenced at Ipswich Crown Court to a whole life order the following day.

The forklift driver, from Erpingham in Norfolk, appealed against the convictions before later deciding to drop the appeal.

The BBC asked police if officers asked Wright to confess to the murders of the five women from Ipswich in light of his guilty plea regarding Victoria.

"He was not asked again about the five murders in 2006 for which he has already been convicted," the police spokesperson responded.

articles.title: How Staffordshire reservoir is helping to save the willow tit
articles.summary: Staff at Tittesworth Reservoir are helping to protect the UK's fastest declining resident bird.
articles.body:
Once a thriving and common feature of our woodlands, the willow tit is now the UK's fastest declining resident bird.

According to Severn Trent Water, numbers have fallen by about 96% from 1967 to 2023, with only around 3,400 breeding pairs left across the whole country.

Approximately 10 of those are believed to nest in the grounds of Tittesworth Reservoir, near Leek in Staffordshire.

The site, run by Severn Trent Water, has been trying to improve the outlook for the species as part of its wider initiative to boost the area's biodiversity.

Julian Woolford, chief executive of Staffordshire Wildlife Trust, told BBC Midlands Today: "To have proper management plans in place at Tittesworth for the willow tit is fantastic."

The decline of the bird's population has been put down mainly to urbanisation and the loss of wet woodlands.

It has vanished from most of southern England, but pockets remain in the central part of the country, as well as in Wales and Scotland, according to Severn Trent.

As part of the biodiversity work, staff at the reservoir have been improving the wet woodland habitat.

They have create more dead wood, in which willow tits like to nest, and specially-designed nesting boxes have also been installed.

Graham Osborn, biodiversity and ecology lead at Severn Trent, said: "We inherit this land from future generations so it's really important we give it back in a better condition.

"To know the work we're putting in now is going to improve the habitat for them, and future generations of willow tit, is a fantastic achievement. For us to be able to put a stamp on that and to really drive this forward."

For its work to improve habitats in the area, Tittesworth was awarded The Wildlife Trust's biodiversity benchmark accreditation in July.

As a result, the 145-hectare (358-acre) reservoir site became the largest of its kind in the UK to receive the recognition.

As well as the rare willow tits, Osborn said the site was also home to many mammals, such as bats, badgers, hedgehogs and polecats.

articles.title: In 1968, Canadian Club hid whisky behind Venezuela’s Angel Falls; newlyweds found the case after a jungle trek, one of 25 stashed worldwide
articles.summary: Discover the unique story of David and Diana Mattoon's honeymoon adventure in 1968 as they searched for a hidden case of Canadian Club whisky at Angel Falls, part of an extraordinary marketing campaign that concealed cases worldwide.
articles.body: In 1968, newlyweds David and Diana Mattoon had a very different kind of honeymoon. The newlyweds changed their planned trip to Acapulco and travelled to Venezuela to search for a hidden case of Canadian Club whiskey. Their journey took them into the rainforest near Angel Falls, where they found one of the cases placed around the world as part of an unusual advertising campaign.Canadian Club hid its second whiskey case at Angel Falls in 1968The Hide a Case campaign by Canadian Club started in 1967, when it was under the ownership of Hiram Walker. In this marketing strategy, the firm used to hide cases of Canadian Club and then gave hints to the same, which could be found through advertisements in magazines. According to Rochelle Pereira-Alvares’s thesis, Mickeys, Minis and Punts: An Investigation of the Marketing and Advertising Initiatives of Seagram and Hiram Walker, 1950-1969, archived at Library and Archives Canada, the campaign launched in July 1967, with the first case hidden in Tanzania, close to Mount Kilimanjaro. A second case was hidden at Angel Falls in Venezuela in January 1968. A contemporary report published in The Washington Post on 26 August 1979, by Joseph P. Mastrangelo, titled Whiskey in the Wild, describes the early campaign and what was discovered by two honeymooners, David and Diana Mattoon.David and Diana Mattoon changed their honeymoon plans to find the whiskeyThe couple had earlier planned on having their honeymoon in Acapulco, Mexico. Diana believed they were headed to Acapulco until David revealed his real plan while they were still in the air: to travel to Venezuela and search for the Canadian Club case near Angel Falls. The newlyweds travelled through the rainforest in difficult conditions, encountering heavy rain and mosquitoes along the way. David and Diana were also added to the search by a guide who was called Jungle Rudy. Mastrangelo’s 1979 article says Rudy had earlier helped the advertising team hide the whiskey case. David and Diana found the case within days of starting their trek into the rainforest, according to Mastrangelo’s report.Canadian Club hid 25 whiskey cases between 1967 and 1991The search for the Angel Falls case was just one component of a broad promotion that hid cases of Canadian Club in unexpected places worldwide. Between 1967 and 1991, Canadian Club hid 25 whiskey cases in remote locations around the world, according to VinePair’s article “The Long History of Canadian Club’s ‘Hide a Case’ Campaign.” These hidden cases were found at Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, Angel Falls in Venezuela, the Swiss Alps, the Arctic Circle and Death Valley in California. There were also cases found close to the Great Barrier Reef in Australia and on top of a skyscraper in Manhattan.In an announcement by Canadian Club’s parent Company, Beam Global Spirits & Wine, dated May 17, 2010, it is stated that 16 of the 25 cases had been found by them. The company also said that clues published in their print advertisement in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s aided many people in finding the cases. Canadian Club revived it at different times, allowing people another chance at following the clues.Canadian Club revived the treasure hunt in 2010Hide a Case was revived in May 2010 by Canadian Club and participants in Canada and the United States were challenged to enter a contest with an opportunity to join an expedition around the globe to discover one of the hidden cases and receive a $100,000 reward. As mentioned in the company's press release, World-Famous Treasure Hunt Resurrected, the contest included such challenges as online contests, video submissions and treasure hunting. Four Canadians and four Americans were to be chosen to join an expedition led by television personality Kevin Brauch.The chosen participants were to meet at a secret destination in April 2011 and complete several challenges to uncover the mystery of the lost case. As a result, the old promotion regained popularity through online participation alongside the original search for hidden whiskey. The Mattoons’ honeymoon search for whiskey at Angel Falls, in the Venezuelan rainforest, was among the campaign’s most notable episodes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: AI data centres could undermine UK's net zero goals
articles.summary: Four planned "hyperscale" data centres consider using gas-fired power for their electricity needs.
articles.body:
The UK government's ambition of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 could be undermined by its new deal on AI data centres, according to BBC research.

During Wednesday's Budget speech, Chancellor John Healey said data centres would be allowed to build onsite power generation while they wait for a grid connection.

BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four planned "hyperscale" data centres - including three in the south of England - are already considering using gas-fired power to meet their electricity needs, creating more CO2 than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.

Labour MP Toby Perkins, who chairs the Environmental Audit Select Committee, said a substantial increase in the use of natural gas "can't be the future".

"Government absolutely shouldn't be in the business of just saying anyone who wants to bring it here, can do whatever you like to power it, because that is not acceptable," he said.

The government said data centres were "essential to Britain's economy" and that its new Data Centre Covenant set clear expectations for developers to pay a fair share of the costs they impose on the energy system and deliver benefits for local communities.

Data centres are warehouses full of powerful computer servers used to run a vast range of digital services, including streaming, banking and public services and have been part of the British landscape for more than two decades.

But a new generation of data centres due to come on stream in the next few years will operate on a much larger scale to cope with the growing computing demand needed for increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence technology.

They will consume considerably more energy than their predecessors at a time when the National Grid is already struggling to meet demand.

Ofgem, the energy market regulator, says data centre developers are seeking connections totalling 72 gigawatts. The peak electricity demand across the whole country last year was 45 gigawatts.

Such is the demand for access to the already under-strain national electricity grid, some data centre developers have been told they could be waiting up to 10 years for the system to be upgraded to provide them with a connection.

Nathan McWhinnie, head of market intelligence and oversight at Ofgem, said: "In a lot of places, the grid is at capacity. I think sometimes it's easy to forget the scale of the demand of these connections. These projects are sometimes the size of cities."

In last week's Budget, the chancellor announced a British Data Centre Covenant, requiring operators to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies in return for priority grid connections.

But he also said that where grid connections were unavailable, developers would be permitted to generate their own power on-site.

BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four data centres are already looking at using gas-fired power stations to meet their electricity needs.

If continuously running at full capacity, our calculations show they would require 1.3 gigawatts of power and could produce an estimated 4.1 million tonnes of carbon emissions a year. This could be more than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.

Oliver Hayes, head of campaigns at environmental charity Global Action Plan, said: "If we're powering by gas that means local communities are going to have huge gas turbines on their doorstep, and they are going to be generating a huge amount of local air pollution and a huge amount of noise and they will be using a huge amount of water from the local water supply."

The developments already considering on-site gas vary in scale.

At Acre Slough, west of London, developers say they could use gas engines with a generating capacity of up to 49.5 megawatts while waiting for a National Grid connection, something they expect could take at least 10 years.

At Wapsey's Wood, next to the M40 in Buckinghamshire, a proposed 200-megawatt gas power station could operate until sufficient grid capacity becomes available, currently not expected until 2040.

"It would be a disaster for us environmentally," said Buckinghamshire independent councillor Ed Gemmell, who also leads the Climate Party.

"If allowed, it sets a precedent that we could be getting gas-fired power stations all over the country and that would make it extremely difficult for us to hit any of our environmental and net zero targets."

Quest Park has proposed building a data centre on the site of a quarry pit next to the planned Universal theme park in Bedfordshire. It would have a power load - the total amount of electrical power drawn at any given time - of 1 gigawatt, the equivalent to 200,000–250,000 average UK homes.

David Kohler, director of Quest Park, has previously told the BBC the company's energy mix was still a "work in progress" and that incorporating renewable power was "sensible" but had to be "feasible".

He said creating 1 gigawatt of solar electricity would require an area equivalent to 15% of Bedfordshire, and that wind power was "intermittent and expensive".

He said the company was considering alternative technologies that did not rely on gas combustion.

In Cardiff, a data centre developer is also seeking permission to build a temporary energy centre that has turbines with a maximum generating capacity of 49.9 megawatts.

Planning documents say it could operate for up to five years if the site cannot secure an electricity grid connection quickly enough. Developer Curtis Hall has described the turbine plan as a "worst-case scenario".

All four projects say they intend to connect to the national grid when it can meet their electricity needs, reducing their reliance on fossil fuels.

The government said its priority was connecting data centres to the grid so they could benefit from the UK's rapidly decarbonising power sector.

It said any behind-the-meter power generation would be tightly controlled, time-limited and allowed only for exceptionally strategic projects where sufficient capacity could not be secured by other means.

A government spokesperson added: "Data centres are essential to Britain's economy, supporting everything from online banking to NHS services.

"Pausing development would send jobs, investment and data overseas and leave us more reliant on other countries for critical digital infrastructure. That's why we're backing their growth while making sure it's done responsibly.

"Our new Data Centre Covenant sets clear expectations for developers to minimise water use, pay their fair share of energy costs and deliver benefits for local communities."

articles.title: Somerset villagers 'horrified' by proposed giant solar farm
articles.summary: The company behind the solar farm said it would provide electricity for more than 140,000 homes.
articles.body:
Residents in a village close to a proposed new solar farm say they are "horrified" by the plans.

Solar farm company Low Carbon wants to build the huge development on land around Mark, in Somerset, to help the UK meet its target of being net zero by 2050. It says the project would provide electricity for more than 140,000 homes.

But locals in Mark, a village with a population of about 700 people, say the solar farm is "too large" and the road infrastructure is "not up to scratch".

Ed Perrin, development director at Low Carbon, said the project is at an "early stage" and wants "local knowledge to help shape their plans" ahead of a public consultation next spring.

The project, called Somerset Energy Park , would see the solar farm and an energy storage park built on land east of the M5, have a generating capacity of more than 100 megawatts and would connect to the National Grid.

Jan Horn, who lives in Mark, said: "I'm horrified because they're totally going to encase the village and ruin all the countryside around."

Jane Mason, who has lived in the village for 42 years, said: "I've got very mixed feelings about it.

"I realise we do need to have sustainable electricity. We all need it, people will soon moan when we haven't got it, but equally I worry."

Another local resident, Chris Barrow, said: "The road structure is not up to scratch. The infrastructure is just not there.

"So the roads that would lead to the solar farm are all unclassified roads, single carriageway, country lanes, a lot of right angle bends.

"I just don't know how they're going to actually do the construction and the maintenance."

Rhiannon de Wreede, an expert in renewable energy, said: "We're at the beginning of quite a large energy transition.

"And we're looking to electrify as much as possible to stop burning fossil fuels and really, solar and wind are two of the cheapest ways of generating electricity at the moment."

She said she "understands people's fears" and solar farm projects such as the proposed Somerset Energy Park is "a transition".

"I understand the Mendip Hills are beautiful, and you'll be able to see the solar farm if you're walking in the hills," she said.

"But I also think in the situation that we're at now with the energy. It just feels precarious, our energy supply.

"So anything we can do for the now, we have to seriously consider."

Perrin said solar farm projects across the UK are "absolutely vital" to hit the national net zero target by 2050, meet rising demand, and ensure country is not reliant on energy overseas.

"We completely understand the local area is really important, the Somerset Levels are incredibly important to the people who live there," he said.

"We're undertaking lots of environmental surveys and studies to better understand how the landscape is used, and more importantly how our proposals impact on the landscape to ensure we can incorporate mitigation and alleviate concerns.

"We completely understand local people, with a project of this scale, will have concerns.

"We want to hear those concerns and assure people we're doing a lot of work to try and better understand how we can reduce the impact of our project."

Because of the scale of the development, any final decision will be made by the secretary of state.

Elsewhere in the West, the next stage for what could be one of the UK's biggest solar farms began last month in Wiltshire.

articles.title: What are the rules for drones in the Channel Islands?
articles.summary: The rules around flying drones are in the spotlight after flights were disrupted in Jersey.
articles.body:
After unauthorised drone activity caused flight cancellations in Jersey, authorities say they are reviewing what can be done to prepare for the future.

Flights were affected on Friday and Saturday evening at the island's airport , causing major disruption, and police said an investigation was under way.

There is increasing use of small unmanned aircraft , also known as drones, for filming, photography and light displays, but strict rules were place to keep airspace and maritime space safe and functional.

What rules apply for drone operators in the Channel Islands?

UK and European drone regulations do not apply to the Channel Islands so Jersey, Guernsey, Sark and Alderney have their own air navigation rules .

These apply to airports, harbours, prisons and other sensitive areas, including the Vale Commons Council land in Guernsey.

Drones are not allowed to be flown within two nautical miles of Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney airports unless the Office of the Director of Civil Aviation and the local air traffic control have granted permission.

The harbours and marinas in Jersey and Guernsey require permission from the civil aviation office and the landowner to operate a drone over or within 492ft (150m) of these areas.

The rules around drone use in Sark are overseen by the Chief Pleas and if it grants permission an operator then needs a permit from the Guernsey Director of Civil Aviation.

The Jersey Model Aero Club flying site at Les Landes is currently the only notified site in the island where the operation of powered drones takes place.

A full island no-fly zone is usually in place for all drone activity during air display time periods in the Channel Islands.

The Director of Civil Aviation Jersey Air Traffic Control have developed a code for the use of drones , which states:

Operators are legally responsible for the conduct of the flight

Make sure you can see your drone at all times and can avoid collisions

Do not fly your drone in any way that could endanger people or property

Do not fly higher than 400ft (122m) or within two nautical miles of the airport without the permission of air traffic control

Use your common sense and fly safely, you could be prosecuted if you do not

Drones fitted with cameras must not be flown within 164ft (50m) of people, vehicles or structures or over or within 492ft (150m) of congested areas or large outdoor gatherings such as beaches, concerts and sports events

You need permission for aerial work to use a drone commercially

Elliot Cockett is the managing director of TDR Studio, which provides drone videography services in Guernsey.

He advised people to do their own research before flying a drone.

"You should always ask or try and find out where you can or can't fly a drone," he said.

"There's lots of different players involved in terms of drone safety, which can be a bit confusing."

He said having a common set of rules would be helpful for drone operators.

"I think really the Channel Islands could do with one single consolidated place where people can just go find the information," he said.

"Even as simply as clicking on a map and saying you want to fly here, this is what you've got to avoid, here's the dos and don'ts, here's who you've got to talk to first."

articles.title: James Blunt on Traitors: I tried - and failed - to get banished
articles.summary: The pop star on new music, The Traitors, and what really went down at James Acaster's banishment.
articles.body:
He may have made it to the final episode of this year's Celebrity Traitors, but James Blunt says he did his best to get banished from the show.

The singer-songwriter became a fan favourite for his 1980s leisurewear, outlandish conspiracy theories and military-style approach to tasks.

A dominating presence at the round table, he characterises himself as the "yapping terrier" to actor Michael Sheen's "mature labrador", as they sniffed out the traitors.

Behind the scenes, however, he was playing a different game.

"We all get paid the same, whether you're there for day one or day 23," he tells the BBC.

"So for most of the time, I was trying to... get the hell out of dodge. But no-one was killing me and no-one was banishing me!"

Blunt's cavalier approach informed his gameplay. He knew that outspoken players are often snuffed out first, and that his best bet was to keep a low profile.

"But that's also really boring," he says. "And so for me, I just thought, 'Let's just go around and come up with theories.'

"You don't see it in the edit, but I was telling everyone, 'It doesn't matter [who goes], just kill them all!'

"It's fine, as long as you're apologetic when you get it wrong."

He was wrong more often than he was right. But in the penultimate episode, Blunt and Sheen stumbled on to a theory that the quiet contestants were more suspicious than their outspoken brethren.

In a pivotal round table, they turned their attention towards comedian James Acaster, and picked apart his story of a "murder in plain sight" that had occurred nights earlier.

Caught in the crosshairs, Acaster simply confessed.

"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.

Blunt says there was more to the sequence than viewers realised, hinting that Acaster was caught in a fib about a perfume bottle used in the murderous act.

"He didn't fall on his sword. That's what you saw, that's what you feel, but he didn't.

"You didn't see the full extent of the interrogation. It was heavy in there and it was clear-cut. He was pinned to a post. We got him. We really, really got him.

"I think how that played out hasn't really been revealed to you, but he didn't just say, 'Oh guys, you got me'."

In his exit interview , Acaster admitted the round table had been intense, but laughed off his uncloaking.

"It was sprung on me. It was a surprise," he said. "But I was glad that they caught me."

Blunt says the editing of the TV show is crucial to people's understanding of events.

And, with days and days of footage to sift through, not everything that happens makes it to air.

"There are elements [of the show] where I was screaming at the screen for a different reason than you," he laughs. "No matter what really went on in that castle, you're a victim to the edit."

Still, some of his favourite moments made it into the show, including actress and model Jerry Hall calling him "smooth like butter dripping off of hot corn".

"That was a very special one," he laughs. "And she also said, to my face, 'I'll take you home in your wetsuit'".

And what about Blunt's confession that he greased his nipples with butter before every physical task?

"I'm amazed you don't do that yourself, Mark," he shoots back.

In the end, however, he was voted off the show in its dying moments, when comedian Romesh Ranganathan couldn't shake the idea that Blunt was in cahoots with the traitorous Maya Jama.

Blunt maintains he was blindsided by the accusation, but bears no grudges.

"The ending was perfect. It had all the twists and turns. I wouldn't have wanted it any other way."

Still the question remains. If he wasn't that keen to go the distance in the castle, why did he enter in the first place? Was it simply for the experience, or did he simply want to promote his new music?

"I think you may have hit the nail on the head with the latter," he grins.

"I don't think otherwise I would have signed up to be imprisoned in a castle in Scotland."

There's a method in his madness, though.

In Blunt's own estimation, his eighth album, Airplane Mode, is his best work in years.

Now, musicians make that claim all the time. Blunt himself basically told me the same thing about his last album, 2023's Who We Used To Be.

But this time, he might have a point. After years of chasing radio hits and commercial success, he's gone back to writing from the heart.

The results are much more downbeat than you might expect from a man who's renowned for hilarious social media slapdowns and crowd surfing in inflatable dinghies .

Across the album's 12 tracks, he frequently sounds adrift, fretting about the state of the world and wrestling with "monsters in your head that you can't turn off".

"Darkness came like a tidal wave," he sings on the concerningly titled Reason To Die. "I'm paralysed by my body keeping score," he adds, over the portentous drums of Weight of it All.

The lyrics are informed by those negative, late-night thoughts that prey on your mind when you should be sleeping. Blunt says finally acknowledging them was a relief, after years of "trying to write happy upbeat radio singles".

"I don't have a therapist. I write songs as an exercise in voicing nostalgia and melancholy and the things I struggle with in the world.

"And, you know, the person you talk to the most in the world is the voice in your head. That's the truest conversation you're ever going to have, and that's who I was arguing with in the writing of this.

"I was going over the things that all of us struggle with: the burdens of growing up, growing older, having more responsibilities, having bills to pay, not knowing what the state of the world will be next year."

For all of his flippant humour, Blunt's demons are real.

In his 20s, he was an army captain stationed in Pristina during the brutal Kosovo war, and lost several close friends during the conflict.

Even after he left active service and became a successful musician, he was ostracised and ridiculed by his peers. He was later targeted in a tabloid newspaper sex sting, and was one of the many victims of the News of the World phone-hacking scandal.

The honesty of his new music reflects those experiences. And you can hear the rawness in his voice, too.

The musician who once quipped, " I sing like a girl ", has a new depth to his vocals. On the new song Oh Daisy, there's even a Rod Stewart-esque rasp.

That, he says, is the result of a punishing 21-month tour celebrating the 20th anniversary of his debut album, Back To Bedlam (17.5 million copies sold and counting).

"I really damaged my vocal cords," he says. "I was pushing it too much, and my voice changed as a result.

"I actually now take singing lessons with different people – with an opera singer, even – and the [whole experience] has given my voice a bit of grit.

It's a typically self-deprecating jab. If anyone can laugh at themselves, it's James Blunt. And, however dark his new album gets, there's always a silver lining.

"This is not forever," he counsels himself on the closing track. "It's just for now."

"That song's a fist in the air saying, 'Yeah, we will endure'," says Blunt.

"I think I've been around long enough to know that I don't have to prove anything.

"The record label released my greatest hits album a couple of years ago, so if my greatest hits are already out, what am I doing now?

"I'm a guy on his own, writing songs with nothing to prove. That's a pretty good place to be."

Getting to know the real James Blunt... maybe
